# Application-Specific Extensions


## Overview
Application-Specific Extensions adapt the standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) framework [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md] to solve problems beyond novel-view synthesis of RGB images [G]. They address the limitations of standard 3DGS—such as its reliance on view-dependent spherical harmonics for color and its implicit volumetric representation—by modifying attribute definitions, rendering equations, or post-processing steps [G]. This family includes methods for physical property reconstruction (radiative/tomographic), non-photometric domain adaptation (microscopy, ultrasound), and explicit geometry extraction (meshing) [G].

## Shared principles
All extensions in this family retain the core 3D Gaussian primitive representation: a set of $M$ anisotropic 3D Gaussian kernels $\mathcal{G} = \{G_i\}_{i=1}^M$ [G]. Each kernel is defined by:
*   $\mathbf{p}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$: Position (mean) [G].
*   $\mathbf{R}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$: Rotation matrix [G].
*   $\mathbf{S}_i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}$: Scale matrix [G].
*   The covariance matrix is $\mathbf{\Sigma}_i = \mathbf{R}_i \mathbf{S}_i \mathbf{S}_i^\top \mathbf{R}_i^\top$ [G].

The rendering pipeline's geometric projection remains consistent for ray-based methods: 3D Gaussians are transformed into ray space, and the projected 2D covariance $\mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}_i$ is computed using the Jacobian $J$ of the affine approximation of the projection and the rotation part $W$ of the extrinsic matrix:
$$ \mathbf{\hat{\Sigma}}_i = J W \mathbf{\Sigma}_i W^T J^T $$
[G].

However, the attribute representation and loss functions diverge significantly from the standard RGB opacity/color model [G]. Standard 3DGS uses view-dependent color $\mathbf{c}_i(\mathbf{d})$ [G]. In radiative and domain-specific variants, this is replaced by view-independent scalar attributes or feature vectors [G].

## Subtopics

### [Radiative and Tomographic Gaussians](4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md)
This family adapts 3DGS for X-ray imaging and radiative physics by replacing view-dependent color with view-independent scalar attributes (density or intensity) [4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md]. It solves the problem of reconstructing volumetric density fields or synthesizing X-ray projections from 2D attenuation measurements, where physical attenuation depends on integrated density along the ray path rather than surface appearance [4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md]. Unlike standard 3DGS, which uses spherical harmonics for view-dependent appearance, these methods remove angular dependence to model isotropic radiative transfer [4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md].

### [Domain-Specific Adaptations](5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md)
Domain-Specific Adaptations extend 3DGS to non-photometric domains by replacing view-dependent RGB color with scalar attributes or specialized geometric intersections [5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md]. Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes for novel-view synthesis from calibrated RGB images, these methods optimize against 3D volume data, microscopy stacks, or ultrasound probe planes using domain-specific loss functions and rendering primitives [5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md].

### [Surface and Mesh Extraction](8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md)
This family comprises methods to extract explicit triangular meshes from trained 3DGS models [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md]. Standard 3DGS represents scenes as implicit volumetric primitives, lacking a native surface representation [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md]. These methods solve the problem of obtaining watertight, textured geometry for downstream applications like simulation, AR/VR, or editing [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md]. They differ from sibling methods like [Radiative and Tomographic Gaussians](4971-radiative-and-tomographic-gaussians.md) by focusing on geometric extraction rather than physical property rendering, and from [Domain-Specific Adaptations](5621-domain-specific-adaptations.md) by targeting general mesh generation rather than specific domain constraints like microscopy [8498-surface-and-mesh-extraction.md].

### [Rendering Pipelines and Extensions](8587-rendering-pipelines-and-extensions.md)
This family defines the computational mechanisms that convert a set of 3D Gaussian primitives (or their variants) into 2D images by projecting them onto the camera plane and compositing them [8587-rendering-pipelines-and-extensions.md]. It solves the problem of efficiently rasterizing soft, view-dependent primitives while supporting inverse rendering tasks such as lighting estimation and physical parameter optimization [8587-rendering-pipelines-and-extensions.md]. What sets these methods apart from standard rasterization is the use of alpha blending or weighted-sum compositing over sorted or spatially hashed primitives, often augmented with volume-based occlusion or explicit geometric intersection for sharp features [8587-rendering-pipelines-and-extensions.md].

### 3D Gaussian Splatting for X-ray Projection Rasterization
A rendering technique that leverages 3DGS to rasterize X-ray projections by modeling X-ray attenuation using the Beer-Lambert law, treating the volume as a collection of 3D Gaussians with density and isotropic absorption [S1, unofficial]. The exponential transmittance model $T(t)$ is defined as $T(t) = \exp\left(-\int_{t_0}^t \sigma(\mathbf{r}(s)) ds\right)$, where $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ represents a 3D point along a ray with origin $\mathbf{o}$ and direction $\mathbf{d}$, and $\sigma(\mathbf{p})$ denotes the density at point $\mathbf{p}$ [S1, unofficial]. Color attributes are optional and can be excluded from the rendering model, accounting solely for isotropic absorption [S1, unofficial].

## Background
Originating from the need to apply Gaussian Splatting beyond standard computer graphics, these extensions emerged as the 3DGS framework [2812-3d-gaussian-splatting.md] gained traction for its efficiency [G]. The divergence from photometric rendering began with adaptations for scientific imaging (X-ray, microscopy) and later expanded to explicit geometry extraction to bridge the gap between implicit splats and explicit mesh-based pipelines [G].
